Y's live part mainly describes call transfers, which belong to the conversation rather than to a referral for investigation. X's single DISCRETE part follows the instructions better.

Quoting a charge and taking a deposit or payment are done while the customer is on the line or at the desk, so the activity is almost entirely live. Y's back-office part is vague and its 30% share is not well supported; processing mailed payments is closer to billing-clerk work. X's single LIVE_SERVICE part with a note on later billing set-up fits better.

Contract forms, address changes, and discontinuance orders are all account paperwork entered on the computer, so the statement lists alternative items for one activity rather than different activities. The distinction the instructions call for is where the work is done, and Y splits on that; X's four-way split adds detail not required by the instructions.

Both split live contacts by kind of item; Y's merge of orders and cancellations is reasonable since both are entered and confirmed on the spot. X names the representative as the checker for complaint intake, which fails the requirement that someone else checks or relies on the work, while Y names the staff who act on the complaint.
